title: Let's take a look at Zerywia - An Overland Adventure Game
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jyn59AgDf6o

Daniel (@dungeondive) opens with a warning: Zerywia's rulebook and scenario book are badly written. Learning the game took hours of rereading, the designer's videos and BoardGameGeek threads, some of which contradicted each other. Even so, he's now a convert. It's a Polish Kickstarter adventure game rooted in Slavic myth and the Baltic, where tribe heroes try to save an ancient land from the Murk of the goddess Nyx. A reprint campaign promises rewritten books.

The heart of the game is the saga system. Each hero carries three saga cards (relics, rituals or allies), and each saga unlocks a small deck of story steps: gather journey tokens from forests, ruins and settlements, then sacrifice them for upgrades. He finds it more adventurous than the keyword-collecting of Gloom of Kilforth. Turns run from dawn through night, so you might wait until noon to raid a tomb whose sleepers wake after dark. A hero who dies fully tainted joins the enemy deck as a dread legend, and Kickstarter Legend cards add choose-your-own-adventure interludes between scenarios.

There are four short campaigns that can be chained into one epic, with a true lone-wolf solo mode. The art is dark and metal, and it all fits on his three-by-four table. The flaws are the useless minis, six Kickstarter heroes with no listed starting sagas, and a designer who launched a reprint before writing an FAQ. Like Dungeon Crusade, he calls it frustrating but good, an uphill road to greatness.

----

Zerywia lets you wait for nightfall (or daylight) to tackle a quest on better terms. Do time-of-day systems add real decisions in board games, or just bookkeeping?
